main.title: Devil May Cry
main.summary: Devil May Cry is a 2001 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2.

cards.heading: Devil May Cry
cards.text: Devil May Cry is a 2001 action-adventure game developed and published by Capcom for the PlayStation 2. Set on a remote island, the story centers on Dante, a demon hunter who uses his business to carry out a lifelong vendetta against all demons. He meets a woman named Trish who takes him on a journey to defeat the demon lord Mundus, who is responsible for the deaths of Dante's brother and mother.

cards.heading: Resident Evil gives way to Dante
cards.text: Devil May Cry was conceived by Capcom developers as a possible concept for Resident Evil 4. Due to the staff feeling it would not fit the Resident Evil franchise, the project became its own title. Several gameplay elements were also inspired by a bug found in Onimusha: Warlords. It is very loosely based on the Italian poem Divine Comedy by the use of allusions, including its protagonist Dante (named after Dante Alighieri) and other characters like Trish (Beatrice Portinari) and Vergil or Nelo Angelo (in later games revealed to be a brainwashed Vergil, who represents the Roman poet Virgil).

cards.heading: Demanding action earns critical acclaim
cards.text: Devil May Cry received prominent coverage in the video game media due to the impact it had in the action-adventure genre, its high difficulty, and the high overall scores given to it by professional reviewers. It has sold more than 2.16 million copies, spawned multiple sequels and a prequel, and is considered among the greatest video games ever made.

cards.heading: Stylish combat becomes a genre
cards.text: Devil May Cry would go on to spawn a franchise, consisting of four sequels and a reboot, and two animated series. It has been cited as the beginning of a subgenre of arcade-style hack and slash melee focused action-adventure games called "character action" or "Extreme Combat", which focus on powerful heroes fighting hordes of foes with a focus on stylish action using a variety of attacks and weapons.

main.title: PaRappa the Rapper 2
main.subtitle: Call, response and freestyle
main.summary: PaRappa the Rapper 2 was released for PlayStation 2 in North America on January 23, 2002, after its Japanese debut the previous year.

cards.heading: Call, response and freestyle
cards.text: PaRappa the Rapper 2 reached PlayStation 2 in North America on January 23, 2002, following its Japanese debut the previous year. NanaOn-Sha returns to musical lessons built around call and response. Players follow a teacher's button sequences in rhythm, then work towards the Cool rating through successful improvisation. Changing cadences and remixed lessons give familiar songs new patterns to learn.

cards.heading: Paper characters on PlayStation 2
cards.text: Characters retain their thin, paper-cut appearance within smoother, more detailed environments. PlayStation 2's extra capacity supports animation and musical staging while preserving PaRappa's distinctive silhouette. The contrast between flat performers and a world with depth remains central to the sequel's visual style.

cards.heading: From the lesson to Cool
cards.text: A teacher performs a phrase and a bar displays the buttons for the player's reply. Missed beats lower the rating; a stronger performance can restore it to Good. Musical variations beyond the prescribed sequence can then earn Cool, opening space for freestyle. Learning the lesson supplies the timing needed to improvise around it.

cards.heading: Bonus stages, remixed lessons and versus play
cards.text: After clearing two stages in a row, players can participate in a minigame where they must hit targets held out by Chop Chop Master Onion's Tamanegi students, earning bonus points which are added onto the previous level's score. Clearing each level with a Cool rating unlocks music tracks that can be listened to after completing the game. Each time the player clears the game, the color of PaRappa's hat changes from blue, to pink, to yellow, with each hat remixing the lines in each level. In addition to the single player campaign, the game features a two-player Vs. Mode, in which players are given a line to rap to, which they must improve upon by freestyling better than their opponent.

main.title: Wendy: Every Witch Way
main.subtitle: WayForward · Game Boy Color
main.summary: Wendy: Every Witch Way is WayForward's Game Boy Color platformer starring Wendy the Good Little Witch from the Casper stories. After magical stones disturb a floating castle's gravity, she travels through its halls, gardens, dungeons and towers to put things right. Switching gravity lets Wendy treat the ceiling as another route, changing how an ordinary arrangement of platforms is understood. The player repeatedly reverses the direction of a fall, using the same small space from two perspectives while avoiding the creatures and hazards occupying it.

cards.heading: A young witch turns the route upside down
cards.text: Wendy: Every Witch Way is WayForward's Game Boy Color platformer starring Wendy the Good Little Witch from the Casper stories. After magical stones disturb a floating castle's gravity, she travels through its halls, gardens, dungeons and towers to put things right. Switching gravity lets Wendy treat the ceiling as another route, changing how an ordinary arrangement of platforms is understood. The player repeatedly reverses the direction of a fall, using the same small space from two perspectives while avoiding the creatures and hazards occupying it.

cards.heading: The ceiling can become the next landing
cards.text: A gravity change affects the relationship between Wendy and the architecture around her. A platform that was overhead becomes a possible destination, while another reversal may be needed to leave enough room for the next obstacle. The stages ask the player to plan those changes rather than simply toggle whenever the floor ends. Each world also contains a broom-riding shooting section, giving the journey another pace between the platforming challenges. The familiar witch's equipment and powers provide clear explanations for those different forms of movement.

cards.heading: A late handheld game with another hardware trick
cards.text: Matt Bozon directed and helped design the game, drawing inspiration from the gravity-changing action of Metal Storm. Released in 2001, it also detects when the cartridge is running in a Game Boy Advance and opens an additional world for that machine. The original Game Boy Color adventure remains built around a particularly readable idea: the same room can become another problem when falling changes direction. Wendy's cartoon identity makes that change feel like a natural magical ability, allowing the environments to develop the challenge without requiring a more complicated set of controls.

main.title: Shenmue II
main.subtitle: Learning the streets of Hong Kong
main.summary: Sega released Shenmue II for Dreamcast in Japan on September 6, 2001.

cards.heading: Learning the streets of Hong Kong
cards.text: Sega released Shenmue II for Dreamcast in Japan on September 6, 2001. Yu Suzuki takes Ryo Hazuki from Yokosuka to the busier streets of Hong Kong and the dense buildings of Kowloon. Investigation, work, fighting and Quick Time Events share a city whose shops and residents follow schedules. The sequel expands the journey while allowing players to advance through certain waits between appointments.

cards.heading: Ask directions, learn the city
cards.text: Hong Kong's districts, markets and alleys can initially leave Ryo disoriented. Asking directions and following people helps establish routes between places, while repeated visits make landmarks familiar. Finding a witness therefore also involves learning the city. The larger setting gives Ryo's arrival the practical difficulties of travelling somewhere unfamiliar, with local knowledge built gradually through movement and conversation.

cards.heading: Appointments with less waiting
cards.text: Shops and characters retain their schedules, but certain appointments allow Ryo to advance the clock. This reduces repeated waiting while keeping the hour relevant to an investigation. The sequel can spend more time on the next encounter once the player has found the right place, adjusting the first game's daily rhythm to a broader journey.

cards.heading: Kowloon rises above the streets
cards.text: Kowloon's deteriorating buildings turn exploration into a vertical route through stacked rooms and corridors. Finding a way through these spaces accompanies Ryo's approach to the people he seeks. Action scenes and QTEs gain a more confined setting, contrasting with the earlier markets and streets. Dense architecture helps change the atmosphere as the investigation advances.

main.title: Advance Wars
main.summary: Advance Wars is a turn-based strategy video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance.

cards.heading: Advance Wars
cards.text: Advance Wars is a turn-based strategy video game developed by Intelligent Systems and published by Nintendo for the Game Boy Advance. It is the seventh title in the Wars series of video games, and the first in the Advance Wars sub-series. The game takes place on a fictional continent, where two nations, Orange Star and Blue Moon, have been fighting each other for years. The conflict enters a new stage when an Orange Star commanding officer named Andy is accused of attacking the armies of two other nations, Yellow Comet and Green Earth, without reason, resulting in a worldwide war.

cards.heading: A tutorial brings tactics westward
cards.text: As with previous Wars titles, Advance Wars was not originally intended for release outside Japan, due to Nintendo feeling that Western consumers would not be interested in turn-based games because of their complex mechanics. In order to alleviate this, the developers made the mechanics easy to understand, adding in an in-depth tutorial that did not require players to read the manual. Designer Kentaro Nishimura commented that the game's success shifted Nintendo's attitude over Western tastes, and that same success is frequently credited as a driving force for Nintendo bringing another Intelligent Systems franchise, Fire Emblem, outside of Japan beginning with the seventh installment.

cards.heading: Delayed launches, compilations and a remake
cards.text: Advance Wars was released in North America on September 10, 2001. Its release in Japan and Europe was delayed following the September 11 attacks in the United States. Although eventually released in Europe in January 2002, it would not be released in Japan until the Game Boy Wars Advance 1+2 compilation in 2004 alongside its sequel Advance Wars 2: Black Hole Rising, whose original Japanese release was cancelled. The game received critical acclaim from critics and has been declared as one of the greatest video games ever made. Advance Wars has been re-released for the Wii U Virtual Console simultaneously in Europe and North America on April 3, 2014. On April 21, 2023, the title was remade for the Nintendo Switch alongside its sequel Black Hole Rising in a compilation developed by WayForward titled Advance Wars 1+2: Re-Boot Camp, which was announced by Nintendo at E3 2021. It was released in America and Europe, but not Japan.

main.title: Ooga Booga
main.subtitle: A contest across volcanic islands
main.summary: Ooga Booga is Visual Concepts' multiplayer action game, released for Dreamcast in North America on 11 September 2001.

cards.heading: A contest across volcanic islands
cards.text: Ooga Booga is Visual Concepts' multiplayer action game, released for Dreamcast in North America on 11 September 2001. Players control Kahunas competing for the favour of a volcano goddess across island arenas. Thrown heads, staffs, spells and rideable animals supply a deliberately comic collection of attacks. The four basic characters favour different strengths, from speed to magic, making the choice of fighter part of the contest. Local and online multiplayer put those abilities into direct competition, with the island's creatures and structures offering further opportunities to interfere with rivals.

cards.heading: Claiming help in the arena
cards.text: Boars and birds can be ridden, changing how a player moves through the arena. Tikis provide another useful target: claiming one makes it attack opposing players and their own Tikis. A match therefore involves more than chasing the nearest rival. A helpful animal or captured structure can change the balance, giving somebody away from the main fight a way to return with an advantage. Unlockable characters and islands extend the choices, while the exaggerated movements and attacks keep the contest readable as a shared comic spectacle.

cards.heading: A late online gathering
cards.text: The game arrived near the end of Dreamcast's commercial life and became one of its last original online releases. Visual Concepts was better known on the console for sports games, making this small-scale arena contest a different use of its multiplayer experience. Brian Luzietti and Larry Peacock composed the music. The appeal lies in the temporary opportunities around the island: a rival may appear stronger in a direct exchange, but a mount, spell or newly claimed Tiki can quickly turn the next encounter into a different contest.

main.title: Ace Combat 04: Shattered Skies
main.subtitle: A pilot above Usea
main.summary: Ace Combat 04: Shattered Skies is Namco's PlayStation 2 combat flight game, first released in Japan on 13 September 2001. The player flies as Mobius 1 in a coalition fighting to liberate the continent of Usea from Erusea. This fictional world combines recognisable military aircraft with enormous weapons and a history shaped by falling asteroids. Eighteen campaign missions move between air battles, ground attacks and major installations. In Europe the game appeared as Ace Combat: Distant Thunder, keeping the same campaign under a different subtitle.

cards.heading: A pilot above Usea
cards.text: Ace Combat 04: Shattered Skies is Namco's PlayStation 2 combat flight game, first released in Japan on 13 September 2001. The player flies as Mobius 1 in a coalition fighting to liberate the continent of Usea from Erusea. This fictional world combines recognisable military aircraft with enormous weapons and a history shaped by falling asteroids. Eighteen campaign missions move between air battles, ground attacks and major installations. In Europe the game appeared as Ace Combat: Distant Thunder, keeping the same campaign under a different subtitle.

cards.heading: Choose the aircraft for the assignment
cards.text: Before a sortie, the player selects an aircraft and its special weapon. A mission focused on ground targets asks for different strengths from a battle against enemy fighters. During flight, a radar and target indicators help locate threats while missiles require a suitable approach and lock. The aircraft carry far more weapons than their real counterparts, allowing the action to continue across long engagements. The result balances the recognisable shape and handling of military aviation with missions built around dramatic attacks and rapid changes of target.

cards.heading: The war seen from below
cards.text: Between missions, illustrated story sequences follow a boy living under occupation and his encounters with the enemy pilot Yellow 13. That viewpoint gives the aircraft fought in the sky a connection to life on the ground. Music changes the scale of key encounters, culminating in a choral finale. The AC04 Project team rebuilt the series' approach after Ace Combat 3, earning strong reviews for the controls, presentation and story. Its fictional setting became an important foundation for later entries in the Ace Combat series.

main.title: Wave Race: Blue Storm
main.subtitle: Nintendo Software Technology · GameCube
main.summary: Wave Race: Blue Storm is Nintendo Software Technology's GameCube water-racing game, following Wave Race 64 with new courses, riders and changing weather. Personal watercraft race around buoys while waves continually alter the surface beneath them. The next turn is therefore affected by more than the shape of a fixed track. A swell can lift the craft or disturb an approach, requiring the player to read the water as part of the route. The race remains a contest against other riders, but the sea is an active participant in every lap.

cards.heading: The sea changes the racing line
cards.text: Wave Race: Blue Storm is Nintendo Software Technology's GameCube water-racing game, following Wave Race 64 with new courses, riders and changing weather. Personal watercraft race around buoys while waves continually alter the surface beneath them. The next turn is therefore affected by more than the shape of a fixed track. A swell can lift the craft or disturb an approach, requiring the player to read the water as part of the route. The race remains a contest against other riders, but the sea is an active participant in every lap.

cards.heading: Choose the course with the forecast in mind
cards.text: Championship events provide a weather forecast for their successive days, and the player chooses the order in which available courses are raced. A difficult venue may be more manageable in calmer conditions, making planning part of the sporting challenge before the start. Correctly passing coloured buoys builds the turbo meter, while a missed buoy costs that accumulated progress. The rider balances the prescribed route against opportunities to accelerate, with the weather influencing how confidently a familiar sequence of corners can be attempted.

cards.heading: A launch game built around moving water
cards.text: Released with the GameCube in Japan in 2001, Blue Storm gave the console a showcase for a landscape that moves beneath the player. Different riders bring their own handling characteristics, and multiplayer lets a group contest the courses together. Lawrence Schwedler and James Phillipsen composed the music. Its central pleasure remains learning how to cooperate with an unstable surface. A fast lap depends on making the machine work with the water's movement, recognising when to commit to a turn and when the next wave requires an adjustment.

main.title: Nintendo GameCube
main.subtitle: Small discs and a distinctive controller
main.summary: On September 14, 2001, Nintendo launched GameCube in Japan.

cards.heading: Small discs and a distinctive controller
cards.text: Nintendo launched GameCube in Japan on September 14, 2001. A compact case houses the IBM Gekko processor and Flipper graphics chip, with four controller ports on the front and a drive for eight-centimetre optical discs. Its controller groups differently shaped buttons around a large A button. Luigi's Mansion and Wave Race: Blue Storm accompanied the Japanese launch; a later Game Boy Advance link cable extended the console's possibilities across two screens.

cards.heading: A button at the centre
cards.text: The large A button forms the centre of the controller's right-hand cluster. B, X and Y occupy distinct positions and have different shapes, helping the thumb recognise actions by touch. Two grips, an analogue stick, C Stick, analogue triggers and built-in rumble complete the arrangement. The layout gives a primary action a clear physical position while keeping other commands nearby.

cards.heading: An eight-centimetre optical disc
cards.text: The proprietary optical disc measures eight centimetres and holds about 1.5 GB. Nintendo specified a CAV system and average access times around 128 milliseconds. Its capacity allows much more audio, texture and other data than common Nintendo 64 cartridges, while the small format retains a distinct physical identity. The top-opening lid makes inserting that disc part of the console's everyday use.

cards.heading: Gekko and Flipper
cards.text: A 485 MHz IBM PowerPC Gekko processor works alongside the Flipper system LSI, developed with ArtX and manufactured by NEC. The architecture includes low-latency 1T-SRAM and dedicated framebuffer and texture caches. Nintendo emphasised predictable performance in actual development, aiming to reduce bottlenecks as studios built and tested games for the new machine.

cards.heading: A handle and four controller ports
cards.text: The case measures about 15 centimetres wide, 11 high and 16.1 deep. A rear handle makes it easy to carry, and four front ports prepare it for local multiplayer without an extra adapter. The Japanese launch model's violet finish reinforces its conspicuous shape. Case, handle and ports give the console a practical identity as something to bring to a shared game.

cards.heading: Luigi and Wave Race at launch
cards.text: Luigi's Mansion and Wave Race: Blue Storm show different uses for the hardware at the Japanese launch. Lighting, transparency and facial animation give Luigi's ghost-filled adventure its atmosphere. Wave Race instead concentrates on water, speed and changing weather. The two games introduce the machine through different kinds of surfaces and movement.

cards.heading: A cable between two screens
cards.text: Released in Japan in December 2001, the Game Boy Advance link cable lets compatible games use the handheld as a controller, second screen or device for transferring data. Television and handheld can display different information, and some software temporarily downloads content to the GBA. Later games developed cooperation and private information around this arrangement, extending play beyond one shared display.
